passage_support.leg: A1 — the Hittite term for the headgear (textual register)
passage_support.source: Hoffner, H. A. Jr., 'An Anatolian Cult Term in Ugaritic', JNES 23/1 (Jan. 1964), 66-68
passage_support.source_kind: scholarly-article (peer-reviewed journal; text quoted from the author's collected-writings scan)
passage_support.locator: p. 67 body text and note 16 (artifact hoffner-djvu.txt lines 434-438, 455-457)
passage_support.reading: The Hittite term for the headgear is kupaḫi- (Hoffner's phrasing: 'which denotes a type of headgear'), for which Hoffner proposes an Anatolian loan into Hebrew qōba‘ ('helmet, headgear') and, following Gaster (1930s), relates to an alphabetic transcription; note 16 cites A. Goetze, 'Hittite Dress', Corolla Linguistica, p. 59, for the list-equation kupaḫi = TÚG SAG.DUL.
passage_support.supports: The entry's requirement to keep 'textual garment term' separate from 'depicted garment': the Hittite headgear word is written with the textile classifier TÚG (cloth) in lexical lists, i.e. the Hittites' own naming is a cloth head-covering term and does not by itself licence a metal 'helmet/crown' reading; the modern/Greek-comparative naming rests on a scholarly hypothesis chain (Gaster 1930s; Hoffner 1964) rather than on a preserved object.
passage_support.does_not_support: It does not identify any depicted figure, any specific tablet, or the horned divine crown as such; the Hebrew/Greek comparison is explicitly a hypothesis ('we might wish to posit').

passage_support.leg: A2 — gender-contrast in the same terminology
passage_support.source: Hoffner, H. A. Jr., 'Symbols for Masculinity and Feminity', JBL 85/3 (Sep. 1966), 326-334
passage_support.locator: p. 331 body text (prayer to Ištar of Nineveh) and note 33 (artifact lines 2309-2313, 2330)
passage_support.reading: The women's headgear is TÚG kureššar, established by Hoffner from two independent lines of evidence (the soldier's-oath list equation TÚG.NÍG.MUNUS = TÚG kureššar and the kulessar/kuressar alternation); the men's headgear is kupaḫi- (again citing Goetze 'Hittite Dress' p. 59).
passage_support.supports: The entry's male/female divine-figure contrast (lines 135-136) at the level of textual terms rather than only depicted silhouettes; also the entry's discipline 'distinguish depicted garment / textual garment term / excavated textile / reconstructed cut'.
passage_support.does_not_support: Nothing here dates either term or ties it to a specific relief; the OCR of this scan renders the word as 'kupafri-' and the digraph forms are mangled (see quote_fidelity).

passage_support.leg: B — the royal headgear register: named images and a written term
passage_support.locator: p. 95 left column (artifact lines 477-486), p. 116 left+right columns (lines 1357-1368)
passage_support.reading: Late Bronze Age Anatolian headbands are attested both in depictions and in texts: they 'may be seen on a number of official Hittite depictions' and are 'found on kings: Tudhaliya IV from Yazilikaya (scene from Room 64), royal couple on an Alacahöyük orthostat, Muwatalli II on a relief from Sirkeli, and on the Sun god in a depiction from Hattuša (Südburg...)'; the Hittite inventory term lupan(n)i is interpreted (Vigo) as a fabric worn on the head, 'sometimes … made of gold, silver, "black iron" or bronze', and read as the head adornment of priests/priestesses and possibly of rulers in their high-priest role.
passage_support.supports: Independent convergence with the round-8 Bonatz leg on relief no. 64 (Tudhaliya IV) from a different genre/venue, and it names a *textual* royal/priestly headband term — so the entry's line-137 royal row can carry 'depicted headband + named kings + inventory term' rather than a single 'rounded cap' paraphrase.
passage_support.does_not_support: It does not describe the horned cap, and the entry's literal 'rounded cap' wording is not the terminology used here; the lupan(n)i interpretation is quoted at second hand from Vigo 2010 (not retrieved this round -> to-verify).

passage_support.leg: C — the earlier (pre-Hittite) object register, dated
passage_support.source: Wygnańska 2014, PAM 23/2: 93-95; Zimmermann, Anodos 6-7 (2006-2007): 511; Simpson, Brill 2018: 666
passage_support.reading: Pre-Hittite central Anatolia has a dated elite head-adornment tradition: openwork headbands at Alacahöyük that 'probably functioned as a crown' and diadems found 'in a restricted number of elite burials … clearly attributes of power and elevated social position'; diadems 'mostly of gold, proliferated in Anatolia in the second half of the 3rd millennium BC'; the 13 Alacahöyük Royal Tombs are dated (Zimmermann's calibrated bracket: upper limit c. 2300 BC cal., youngest burials c. 2000/1950 BC, 'maximum chronological span') and their metalwork is 'firmly embedded in a Pre-Hittite sequence and cultural environment' yet 'still often erroneously referred to as "Hittite" products'. Simpson independently dates the same tombs to the second half of the third millennium BC and lists gold diadems among their goods.
passage_support.supports: An *earlier* Anatolian headgear comparator with dates and two independent scholarly anchors — but in the headband/diadem register, not the horned-crown register; it also supplies a second naming trap for the entry (calling pre-Hittite Alaca material 'Hittite'), parallel to the entry's line-49 New/Neo-Hittite trap.
passage_support.does_not_support: No pre-Hittite horned or pointed divine crown is depicted, named or catalogued in anything retrieved: the 'earlier Hattic comparator' limb of the residual question therefore stays open (see unresolved_limbs). The 'Hattian' ethnic attribution of the tombs is a modern convention rather than a claim asserted by these sources.

quote_fidelity.rule: Quoted passages preserve the bytes of the retrieved artifacts; every departure is disclosed here.
normalizations: Hoffner scan OCR forms are preserved in the artifact_form fields and normalized in the reading fields: 'Jcupahi'->kupaḫi, 'Jcubagi'->kubagi, 'kupafri'->kupaḫi, 'hupahi'->kupaḫi, 'TtJG'->TÚG, 'NlG'->NÍG; the OCR 'g' rendered as '</' in line 435 ('“</” laryngeal' for '“g” laryngeal').

Line-final hyphenation of the two-column OCR is joined in the quotes ('contain-ed'->contained, 'Küçük-höyuk'->Küçükhöyuk); the one counter-case is handled explicitly: 'Jcubagi-' + 'for' is kept apart because the hyphen belongs to the word (Q_H2).

PAM pages 92-95 and 115-116 are two-column: the pdftotext pages interleave the right column between left-column lines. Quotes from those pages are the contiguous column text; the containment test was run against a column reconstruction of the page region (disclosed per quote in tested_against), and the result of the same test against the raw interleaved text is recorded as longest_ngram_raw_interleaved (it necessarily fails, 8-10 tokens, and that failure is the evidence for the interleave).

Printed footnote markers (16, 17, 33, 22, 7) and the page-break duplication in the djvu text are omitted from quotes; source-internal quotation marks are normalized to single quotes inside JSON strings; Greek/Hebrew words that the OCR dropped entirely are shown as '…' with a note (Hoffner note 17 carries such a drop).
Source-internal italics and small caps are not marked; ephemeral page headers/footers are excluded from quotes and used only as page locators.

quote_verification.method: Automated containment test over vectorized tokens: both the quote and the artifact text are NFKC-normalized, the disclosed OCR mapping is applied, diacritics are folded, lowercased, non-alphanumerics dropped; then the longest contiguous token n-gram of the quote found in the artifact is measured (mirroring the sibling verifier's >=10-token pass rule).

support_scope: Bounded to the alternate angle.
